title: Protest of Google LLC regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s Interim Resource Adequacy Service and Large Load Registry proposal under ER26-3515.

documents.name: Protest of Google LLC - ER26-3515-000.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                  )
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                      )         Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                  )

                               PROTEST OF GOOGLE LLC

       Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 Google LLC (“Google”) hereby submits this protest

regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”)

and Large Load Registry proposal.

       Google’s concerns with IRAS center on the proposed mechanism, not the underlying

objectives. Specifically, Google agrees that New Large Loads that do not bring sufficient new

capacity to offset their expected demand should be subject to curtailment prior to other firm

wholesale customers during tight system conditions, ensuring service to residential and other

commercial customers remains reliable. Consistent with this principle, a longstanding and

foundational pillar of Google’s energy procurement philoso phy has been that Google should

enable sufficient new capacity to meet its energy demand.

       IRAS would stymie that goal. It would inject fresh uncertainty into PJM, threatening

desperately needed investments to build out the region’s generation fleet. The fundamental flaw

in IRAS is PJM’s proposal to assign general curtailment obligations to Electric Distributors

(“EDs”) with New Large Loads that do not bring new capacity, despite lacking jurisdictio n over

how EDs execute those curtailments.. Consequently, in the event of a shortage, New Large Loads



   1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2026).
 that bring new capacity—and spend billions of dollars doing so—could still be curtailed before

those that do not. PJM cannot resolve this basic misalignment because curtailment priority among

end users is a quintessential retail ratemaking question that o nly states have the authority to

implement under the Federal Power Act (“FPA”).

         Nevertheless, because of that misalignment, IRAS creates a clear risk that New Large

Loads that invest billions of dollars to bring their own new capacity —i.e., the purported means of

avoiding curtailment under IRAS——will, in fact, not avoid it. By penalizing the very behavior

it seeks to incentivize, IRAS directly undercuts its own foundational premise. That regulatory

disconnect makes it extremely risky for Google and similarly situated customers to invest in new

PJM capacity unless and until states enact prompt laws or regulations establishing consistent

curtailment protections. Ultimately, the result of IRAS will be less investment in new capacity in

PJM—the exact opposite of what the region needs. Accordingly, the Commission should

emphatically reject a proposal that would actively deter the capacity investments PJM so urgently

needs.

         In addition, IRAS violates the FPA in several different respects. It exceeds the

Commission’s jurisdiction, it is unduly discriminatory, and it is unjust and unreasonable. Any of

those significant shortcomings would be sufficient, on its own, to overturn a Commission approval

on appeal. The long shadow of uncertainty caused by litigation over a program with such obvious

shortcomings will further sap the confidence necessary for companies like Google to deploy the

capital needed to develop the gigawatts (“GW”) of new generation that PJM demands.

         IRAS is a deeply flawed approach in light of the many, superior ways of addressing the

concerns that motivated PJM to pursue IRAS in the first place. Specifically, because the

curtailment issue is a quintessential question of state law, PJM should pursue an actual program



                                                   -2-
      of “cooperative federalism” through which it uses its position as operator of the wholesale market

     to empower the states to effectuate curtailment priorities that meet their public policy priorities,

     including, for example, a preference for New Large Loads that bring their own new capacity. This

     would avoid the legal risk and uncertainty that would throttle investment in new generation

     capacity while providing a clear path to pursuing the goals purportedly underlying this proceeding.

     Moreover, there are several additional options, such as demand response reforms, to unlock the

     flexibility that data centers and other large loads can provide under the appropriate circumstances

     that could further improve PJM’s capacity position without the problems that IRAS presents.

     Accordingly, for the reasons that follow, the Commission should accept the Large Load Registry

     (the only legally defensible part of PJM’s proposal), while rejecting IRAS and directing PJM onto

     a different, more sustainable path that will actually improve resource adequacy in the region to the

     benefit of all stakeholders, including retail customers.

I.       WHO WE ARE

             Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible

     and useful. AI is critical to that mission. Data centers are the infrastructure that make AI possible,

     and electricity is the fuel that powers them.         To serve Google’s customers, data center

     infrastructure consumes a large amount of electricity and requires reliable electric service to

     operate. As Google’s business grows, so too does its demand for reliable, affordable, and clean

     electricity.

II.      PROTEST

         A. IRAS Will Not Incentivize New Large Loads to Bring Their Own New Capacity

             Google agrees with the principle that ostensibly underlies IRAS. Namely, New Large

     Loads that connect to the transmission system should be incentivized to bring new capacity to the

     region to cure resource adequacy shortcomings; those that do not should be curtailed at the
                                                          -3-
 appropriate time. If the Commission agrees with that principle, it should reject IRAS. That is

because PJM legally cannot ensure that New Large Loads that utilize the Bring Your Own New

Capacity (“BYONC”) pathway will receive firm service and not be curtailed, as PJM itself

acknowledges. 2 Instead, it is the states that have “‘exclusive jurisdiction’ . . . to ensure that the

appropriate retail customers, i.e., New Large Loads, including data centers—and not residential

customers or small industrial customers—are reduced when system conditions call for PJM to

require load reductions.” 3 PJM is explicit that it has no authority to ensure that New Large Loads

get the purported benefit of the IRAS “bargain” (firm service), explaining that it is “leaving it to

[EDs], in coordination with the appropriate states and/or [Relevant Electric Reta il Regulatory

Authorities, (“RERRAs”)], [Load Serving Entities, (“LSEs”)], and LSE customers to determine

which loads should ultimately reduce subject to IRAS.” 4

        States might curtail loads in the order that PJM envisions, but there is no guarantee. A

state could create its own retail curtailment scheme that reflects entirely different considerations

than IRAS. For example, a state could establish a curtailment priority that gives effect only to new

capacity within the state or that meets certain other limiting characteristics. Or, alternatively, a

state may curtail a New Large Load that brings new capacity in favor of other retail customers,

including data centers, that are deemed too important to be curtailed. In short, it is impossible to




        2 Compare PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim
Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515, at 2
(filed Aug. 13, 2026) (“Transmittal”)Transmittal at 2 (“New Large Loads can avoid t his condition on taking
transmission service by bringing new capacity to the system.”), with Transmittal at 87 (“[W]hile PJM will determine
the quantity of MW that load in a zone/area will need to be reduced by to maintain system reliability in the PJM
Region, states may determine—under their own laws, policies, and definition of what constitutes ‘large load’—which
resources will be called on to reduce load.”).
        3Id. at 90-91

        4 Id. at 92.



                                                            -4-
 know whether the states will implement IRAS as PJM expects because “the curtailment protocol

was not developed with [relevant state actors’] input.” 5

        As a result, IRAS severely undermines any incentive to invest in new generation. If entities

are going to spend billions of dollars to offset curtailment risk by bringing their own new capacity,

and improve the region’s resource adequacy shortfall, they need some assurance that they will, in

fact, receive firm service and will not be curtailed whenever conditions are tight. To be clear:

Google is prepared to invest the billions of dollars necessary to ensure that its New Large Loads

bring adequate new capacity. Maintaining regional resource adequacy has been and remains a

longstanding and foundational pillar of Google’s energy procurement philosophy. 6 But Google

cannot responsibly do so without some assurance that it will receive firm retail service in exchange

for those investments, particularly where PJM’s proposal threatens to unwind firm service for

facilities that have already executed firm Energy Service Agreements (“ESAs”). Without that

assurance—which, again, PJM is legally precluded from providing—BYONC is a gamble, not an

investment.

        And that is not the only source of uncertainty inherent in IRAS. As explained below, IRAS

has several glaring legal flaws. As PJM’s own staff recognized when it recommended against

pursuing the previous—albeit substantially similar—iteration of IRAS, the inevitable litigation

that follows such a legally infirm proposal will be significant and ultimately undermine the




        5 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Answer of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission in support of the
Organization of PJM States, Inc.’s motion for extension of time, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, at 2 (filed on Sep. 1,
2026).
        6 See, e.g., Google, The Clean Transition Tariff, https://www.gstatic.com/marketing-
cms/1f/d3/00f64e2c4f4f92e8e34ed8ef1e2c/clean -transition-tariff-ctt.pdf (last visited Sept. 1, 2026).

                                                           -5-
 program’s ability to achieve its purported objectives. 7 Inevitable litigation coupled with IRAS’s

obvious legal flaws will cast a pall of uncertainty over the contracting for and development of new

capacity in PJM for as long as this proceeding and the resulting appeals continue. The best thing

that the Commission could do to create certainty and facilitate investment in new long-term

capacity is to reject IRAS emphatically (while accepting the Large Load Registry) and have PJM

promptly produce a proposal that complies with the FPA. Anything short of that will only deepen

the current resource adequacy insecurity in PJM.

         PJM’s attempt to justify IRAS with analogies to various constructs that the Commission

has accepted cannot bear the weight PJM puts on them. For example, the Southwest Power Pool’s

(“SPP”) “large load integration construct”—which includes SPP’s High Impact Large Load

Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”) 8—is an inapt comparison that only highlights IRAS’s faulty

premise. Under HILLGA, new generation paired with an electrically proximate large load can opt

to interconnect to SPP’s system on an expedited basis in exchange for interconnection service that

is limited in ways explicitly spelled out in the SPP tariff. 9 And because SPP has authority over

generator interconnection in the region, it can actually deliver the promised benefits of HILLGA.

In this way, entities considering deploying capital in SPP know exactly what they are getting if

they participate in HILLGA, which is essential for unlocking investment on the scale needed to

bolster resource adequacy. IRAS does not offer comparable predictability because PJM has no

authority over which retail loads are curtailed. 10 As noted above, this means that large loads in


       7 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., CIFP Connect & Manage: PJM Stage 4 Proposal Executive Summary
(June 30, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-
item-02a---pjm-stage-4-proposal---connect-and-manage---executive-summary.pdf.
         8 Transmittal at 21-22 n. 64 (citing Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031 (2026)).

         9 Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031 at P 8.

         10 See Transmittal at 85 (“[T]oday Electric Distributors select, consistent with their state programs, which
loads to reduce in response to a PJM load reduction directive. . . . PJM is not looking to change any existing approach.

                                                              -6-
 PJM could invest billions of dollars to develop new generation only to be curtailed by an ED that

has no obligation to prioritize service to New Large Loads that bring their own new capacity.

         Google has already committed to “build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and

electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources

whether by building, or buying from, new or otherwise additive power pla nts.”11 And it is not

alone. Indeed, there is no shortage of offtakers willing to enter long-term contracts for new

capacity, provided that they have certainty over the benefits that they will receive in return. PJM

should focus on providing that certainty rather than undermin ing the otherwise favorable

investment conditions for companies that stand ready to make the commitments that will actually

bring new capacity to the region.

    B. IRAS Violates the FPA

         IRAS is also illegal for three independent reasons. First, it aims at and targets the retail

sphere, in violation of the FPA’s division of jurisdiction. Second, it is unduly discriminatory

because it treats entities that are functionally identical for th e purposes of the wholesale market

differently without any legally relevant basis for doing so. Suffice it to say, discrimination on the

basis of legally irrelevant characteristics can never be “due.” Finally, it is unjust and unreasonable

because PJM would charge customers for capacity that it never intends to procure or that those

customers, by design, can never use.




Currently, the manner in which an Electric Distributor reduces load is a function of their state-approved contracts and
state-approved curtailment and load reduction plans.”).
         11 The White House, Ratepayer Protection Pledge (Mar. 4, 2026), https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/20
26/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.

                                                              -7-
              1. IRAS Exceeds the Commission’s Jurisdiction

        IRAS exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction because it targets particular retail

customers: “New Large Loads.” FPA Section 201(b) “‘limit[s] FERC’s sale jurisdiction to that

at wholesale,’ reserving regulatory authority over retail sales (as well as intras tate wholesale

sales) to the States.” 12 “FERC cannot take an action transgressing that limit no matter how

direct, or dramatic, its impact on wholesale rates.” 13 To respect that limit, FERC and entities like

PJM are prohibited from taking actions that “aim[]” at or “target” particular retail consumers or

the retail market generally. 14 Instead, as relevant here, a Commission order adheres to the FPA’s

jurisdictional divide only where “every aspect of the regulatory plan happens exclusively on the

wholesale market and governs exclusively that market’s rules.” 15

        IRAS violates that principle. FERC cannot approve tariff provisions where retail

consumers are the “target at which [those tariff provisions] aim.” 16 IRAS breaks that rule

because it targets retail customers by assigning the wholesale curtailment obligation based on the

size (i.e., more than 50 MW) and vintage (i.e., in-service date and ramp rate) of the relevant

retail customers.17 In so doing, the proposal makes the characteristics of the retail customer, not

that of the ED, LSE, or Eligible Customer, or any other Commission -jurisdictional entity or

transaction, the basis for imposing a curtailment obligation. It thus explicitly determines the




        12 FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 279 (2016) (“EPSA”) (quoting New York v. FERC, 535
U.S. 1, 6 (2002)).
        13 Id. at 280.

        14 Id. at 282 (quoting Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U.S. 373, 385 (2015) “Oneok”)).

        15 Id.

        16 Oneok, 575 U.S. at 385; see EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.

        17 Transmittal at 6.



                                                         -8-
 quality of wholesale service based on the characteristics of retail customers, and, as explained

below, that is no accident or side effect of IRAS; it is the entire reason we are here. 18

         Compare that “target[ing]” of individual retail customers to what PJM is not doing.

Although PJM suggests that the policy problem it is trying to solve is capacity shortages driven by

new load growth, 19 under IRAS, PJM would not determine an ED’s curtailment obligations based

on its rate of load growth. Consider a hypothetical where one ED’s annual load grows by 200 MW

through ten separate 20 MW industrial facilities, while another ED’s load grows by only 100 MW

driven by one single data center. Assume none of the loads bring their own new capacity. The

first ED would not be subject to curtailment while the second ED would , despite having half the

load growth of the first. That differential treatment confirms that it is not the ED’s load growth

that is the focus of IRAS, but rather the specific retail customers that make up that load growth

that matters. To put it mildly, this is not a regulation where “every aspect of the regulatory plan

happens exclusively on the wholesale market and governs exclusively that market’s rules.” 20

Rather, IRAS is unlawfully “tethered” to the retail markets and specific retail consumers 21—most

prominently, new data centers. 22




         18 Cf. Corner Post, Inc. v. Bd. of Governors of Fed. Rsrv. Sys., 603 U.S. 799, 815 (2024) (“As this Court has
repeatedly stated, the text of a law controls over purported legislative intentions unmoored from any statutory text.”);
Keister v. AARP Benefits Comm., 410 F. Supp. 3d 244, 257 (D.D.C. 2019) (“[I]t is well established that extrinsic
evidence may not be relied upon to show the subjective intent of the parties absent ambiguity in the contract’s
language.” (cleaned up)).
         19 See, e.g., Transmittal at 99, 124.

         20 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.

         21 Cf. Hughes v. Talen Energy, Mktg. LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 166 (2016) (state’s action to encourage
development of certain generation resources cannot be tethered to the resource’s wholesale market participation).
         22 PJM’s own transmittal letter confirms that the target of IRAS is specific retail customers.      See, e.g.,
Transmittal at 17 (explaining that, as directed by the PJM Board, one of the elements of PJM’s proposal is that “IRAS
will be applicable to ‘[N]ew Large Loads that, as of June 1, 2027, do not bring sufficient capacity to serve their
resource adequacy needs and cannot otherwise be served at the 1-in-10 reliability standard[.]”).

                                                              -9-
          PJM’s arguments to the contrary are barred by governing Supreme Court precedent.

PJM briefly claims that, as in EPSA, the policy question at issue is one the FPA’s drafters “could

not have anticipated.”23 But novel circumstances are not an excuse to rewrite a statute. 24 PJM

does not and cannot even assert that it satisfies EPSA’s requirement that the regulation

“addresses—and addresses only—transactions occurring on the wholesale market.” 25

         Nor does it help that, after determining that an ED must “reduce load by a certain MW

quantity” based on the characteristics of its retail customers, PJM then leaves it to the ED and state

to implement the reduction across its customers. 26 Although PJM attempting to direct reductions

on a customer-by-customer basis would provide another reason why IRAS is unlawful, the fact

that things could be more jurisdictionally infirm does not immunize PJM’s already-unlawful

proposal to condition curtailment obligations on retail customer characteristics, rather than

consumer-neutral load and capacity considerations. The plan still targets and is tethered to specific

retail consumers and thus exceeds PJM’s jurisdiction. 27

         Similarly, it is no answer for PJM to assert that IRAS’s targeting of data centers is justified

because they make up the vast majority of load growth. While that is true, the fact that certain

retail customers are having an outsized effect on the wholesale market does not give the

Commission license to target those customers any more than it gives it license to target “markets

in all electricity’s inputs—steel, fuel, and labor most prominent among them—[based on how they]


         23 Transmittal at 91.

         24 Cf. Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. 629, 649 (2022) (refusing to “rewrite a constitutionally valid
statutory text under the banner of speculation about what Congress might have done had it faced a question that ... it
never faced”).
         25 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282; see Transmittal at 91 (drawing comparison to EPSA as to whether the policy need

was anticipated, but not whether the regulation only addresses wholesale transactions).
         26 Transmittal at 92.

         27 Oneok, 575 U.S. at 385; see EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.



                                                             -10-
 affect generators’ supply of power.” 28 Rather, as discussed above, the Commission must restrict

its program of regulation to the wholesale market, no matter how significantly certain retail

customers’ demand might affect that market and make retail regulation a tempting target for the

Commission.

        Finally, although PJM characterizes its proposal as “a product of cooperative federalism,”

it is, in fact, quite the opposite. Cooperative federalism is rooted in the concept that the federal

entity need not, and should not, exercise the full extent of its authority when addressing issues

that affect both federal and state interests. For example, in EPSA, while the Commission claimed

that it could negate state decisions prohibiting retail consumers from making wholesale demand

response bids, it “chose not to do so in recognition of the linkage between wholesale and retail

markets and the States’ role in overseeing retail sales.” That was a scheme of cooperative

federalism in “which the States retain[ed] the last word.” Here, by contrast, PJM has created a

scheme that it lacks the authority to carry out and so it has, instead, unilaterally foisted onto the

states the responsibility for implementing IRAS without consulting with them on the program’s

design.29 The principle of cooperative federalism does not describe a program that would have

the federal government exceed its authority and then leave it to the states to resolve the resulting

complexities.

             2. IRAS Is Unduly Discriminatory

        IRAS is unduly discriminatory for similar reasons. The FPA categorically prohibits

undue discrimination, which occurs when similarly situated entities are treated differently


        28 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 277-78.

        29 See PJM Interconnection, Answer of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission in support of the
Organization of PJM States, Inc.’s motion for extension of time, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, at 2 (filed on Sep. 1,
2026) (“The curtailment protocol was not developed with PA PUC’s input, and it may impinge upon our jurisdiction
over retail rates.”).

                                                          -11-
 without good reason. 30 When evaluating whether resources are similarly situated, it is not enough

for those resources to be different in any respect; rather, they must be different with respect to

the inquiry at hand. 31 As explained above, the only differences between EDs that receive

curtailment orders under IRAS and those that do not are the characteristics of their retail

customers, which are outside Commission jurisdiction and thus legally irrelevant to the question

of whether two entities are similarly situated for the purposes of the FPA. Receiving differing

levels of Commission-jurisdictional service based on legally irrelevant differences is unduly

discriminatory.

       But even if PJM could consider the characteristics of retail customers when making

curtailment decisions, IRAS would still be unduly discriminatory because it discriminates

amongst EDs for reasons that have nothing to do with the resource adequacy concerns PJM is

trying to address.

       First, under IRAS, PJM would issue curtailment directives to EDs based on the size of

individual new loads rather than the aggregate amount of new demand in a zone. It is the

aggregate growth that causes a resource adequacy challenge, not the load growth of only a subset

of customers. To slightly revise the example from the previous section, if a hypothetical ED’s

load grows by 200 MW due to ten 20 MW loads, it would have no curtailment exposure under

IRAS. If another hypothetical ED’s load grows by 200 MW based on a single data center, all the

incremental load would be subject to IRAS despite having identical load growth to the first ED.

PJM has not explained how such disparate treatment can be justified under the FPA.




       30 Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y., Inc. v. FERC, 45 F.4th 265, 282 (D.C. Cir. 2022).

       31 See Xcel Energy Servs., Inc. v. FERC, 41 F.4th 548, 559-60 (D.C. Cir. 2022).



                                                       -12-
        In addition, IRAS is unduly discriminatory because of the manner in which it treats New

Large Loads differently than existing large loads. One MW of load contributes identically to a

reliability requirement shortfall regardless of its in-service date. Analogous D.C. Circuit and

FERC precedent calls for treating new and continuing customers alike. 32 Nevertheless, PJM

defines a “New Large Load” as having an in-service (or incremental-ramp) date after June 1,

2027. This means that a 500 MW load interconnected in the first half of 2027 would not trigger

a curtailment directive to its ED, but a 500 MW load interconnected in the second half of the

year would. This would be true even though the earlier-in-time load contributes equally to any

resource adequacy shortfall as the later-in-time load. PJM, which bears the burden for justifying

its section 205 proposal, has not explained why large loads that interconnect after June 1, 2027,

warrant differential treatment from those that interconnect before that date, which is reason alone

to reject PJM’s filing.

           3. IRAS Is Unjust and Unreasonable

       Last but not least, IRAS is also unjust and unreasonable for two independent reasons .

First, PJM is proposing to charge customers for a service that it never intends to procure.

Specifically, PJM proposes to exclude from the Variable Resource Requirement Curve (i.e., the

capacity market demand curve) New Large Loads that do not bring the ir own new capacity,

meaning that it would, by definition, not procure capacity to serve them, even if that capacity is

available. Nevertheless, PJM proposes to charge the LSEs that will service those same New

Large Loads for a share of the capacity (even though none of that capacity will have been

procured for them). Being forced to pay money for nothing is not just and reasonable or

consistent with cost causation.


       32 See BNP Paribas Energy Trading GP v. FERC, 743 F.3d 264, 268 (D.C. Cir. 2014).



                                                    -13-
         PJM justifies this novel intervention in the interaction of supply and demand by arguing

that it would help ensure that residential and other existing commercial customers’ rates do not

increase when New Large Loads connect to the grid. 33 To be clear: Google supports that aim

unequivocally. That is why Google signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and, as explained

above, Google is firmly committed to procuring new capacity sufficient to cover its demand. 34

        But breaking supply and demand fundamentals by ignoring the demand that PJM itself

expects to materialize is not a reasonable way to further that critical goal. Most obviously, it

violates the FPA’s cost causation principle, which provides that the costs allocated to an entity

must be “roughly commensurate” to the benefits it receives.35 Cost causation and the statutory

requirement to roughly equate benefits and costs does not permit PJM to assign costs to entities

that are structurally precluded from receiving the corresponding benefits. The fact that New

Large Loads that are curtailed under IRAS might36 receive a credit in their retail rates certainly

cannot retroactively undo PJM’s decision to forgo procuring capacity, but then still charge

customers as if it had, in fact, procured capacity to serve them.

        In addition, ignoring demand to make the market clear is yet another significant intrusion

into the market fundamentals and resulting price signals that, in theory, are the reason the


        33 Transmittal at 23-24.

        34Amanda Peterson Corio, Supporting the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge: Google's Approach
for Responsible Energy Growth, Google: The Keyword (Mar. 4, 2026), https://blog.google/innovation-and-
ai/infrastructure-and-cloud/global-network/affordability-pledge-responsible-energy-growth/ .
          35 See Coal. of MISO Transmission Customers v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1004, 1009 (D.C. Cir. 2022); Long Island
Power Auth. v. FERC, 27 F.4th 705, 714-15 (D.C. Cir. 2022); Neb. Pub. Power Dist. v. FERC, 957 F.3d 932, 939-41
(8th Cir. 2020); Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1260-62 (D.C. Cir. 2018); K N Energy, Inc. v.
FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992).
        36 There is no guarantee that New Large Loads that are curtailed under IRAS will be compensated for those
curtailments, because “how the compensation scheme will work in practice relies on application of state retail law.
Whether a specific New Large Load may be entitled to compensation for provision of IRAS will be determined by
state authorities under state law or [Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities] as may be applicable.”
Transmittal at 106 (footnote omitted)).

                                                           -14-
 Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) exists. 37 In the very short term, PJM’s proposed capacity

market may help achieve the laudable goal of insulating residential and other existing retail

customers from the price effects of large load additions—a goal that, as noted, Google firmly

supports. But it does so only by further balkanizing the market and turning it into a construct

that bears ever-less connection to the economic forces it is supposed to harness. Nominal

reliance on a market-based construct that is in reality untethered to market forces is a recipe for

prolonging PJM’s current resource adequacy crisis or ending up in another one in the future.

        And that is exactly what IRAS would do by removing known, forecasted demand from

the RPM with the explicit goal of reducing resource procurement and resulting capacity prices.

PJM would, once again, be muting the demand signal and forcing capacity price s to a level that

is lower than what is needed to attract investment in new generation. That, in turn, threatens the

region’s long-term resource adequacy and is inconsistent with PJM’s own statement that the

RPM should “reflect actual supply and demand fundamentals.” 38

       Second, IRAS would require EDs with New Large Loads that do not bring their own new

capacity to contribute to the cost of new demand response capacity resources, but curtail the

associated EDs before those demand response resources are dispatched. In oth er words, under

IRAS, New Large Loads would pay for demand response resources to serve as capacity and yet,

when system conditions warrant it, those New Large Loads would be curtailed before demand

response resources are ever dispatched. This defies basic logic: no one would buy an umbrella

on the condition that it must be surrendered the moment it rains, yet that is precisely what PJM

demands here.



       37 Id. at 115 (indicating that the RPM should “reflect actual supply and demand fundamentals”).

       38 Id.



                                                     -15-
         Google reiterates that it is committed to bringing new capacity and supporting legal and

durable solutions for ensuring that large loads do not raise rates or undermine service for

residential customers and other existing customers. Google strongly supports competitive

wholesale markets and believes that they are a highly effective means of developing new supply

while protecting customers from unnecessary costs. But functioning markets require adherence

to market fundamentals. A market design that, like IRAS, undermines the basic principles on

which markets depend is neither just and reasonable nor a viable tool for ensuring resource

adequacy, reliability and affordability.

        C. A Lawful and Durable Framework Can Protect Residential Customers While
        Preserving Incentives for Large Loads to Bring New Capacity

        Accepting IRAS would be an egregious misstep because there are ample alternative

avenues through which PJM, in cooperation with the States, could facilitate the goals underlying

IRAS, rather than impede them.

        First, with the appropriate data management and confidentiality guarantees, the
